On a day-to-day basis, however, the House can also decide to grant individual bills privileged access to the floor, using one of several parliamentary mechanisms. The standing rules of the House include several different parliamentary mechanisms that the body may use to act on bills and resolutions. Which of these will be employed in a given instance usually depends on the extent to which Members want to debate and amend the legislation. In general, all of the procedures of the House permit a majority of Members to work their will without excessive delay. The House considers most legislation by motions to suspend the rules, with limited debate and no floor amendments, with the support of at least two-thirds of the Members voting. Occasionally, the House will choose to consider a measure on the floor by the unanimous consent of Members. The Rules Committee is instrumental in recommending procedures for considering major bills and may propose restrictions on the floor amendments that Members can offer or bar them altogether. Many major bills are first considered in Committee of the Whole before being passed by a simple majority vote of the House. The Committee of the Whole is governed by more flexible procedures than the basic rules of the House, under which a majority can vote to pass a bill after only one hour of debate and with no floor amendments. Although a quorum is supposed to be present on the floor when the House is conducting business, the House assumes a quorum is present unless a quorum call or electronically recorded vote demonstrates that it is not. However, the standing rules preclude quorum calls at most times other than when the House is voting. Questions are first decided by voice vote, although any Member may then demand a division vote. Before the final result of a voice or division vote is announced, Members can secure an electronically recorded vote instead if enough Members desire it or if a quorum is not present in the House. The constitutional requirements for making law mean that each chamber must pass the same measure with the identical text before transmitting it to the President for his consideration. When the second chamber of Congress amends a measure sent to it by the first chamber, the two chambers must resolve legislative differences to meet this requirement. This can be accomplished by shuttling the bill back and forth between the House and Senate, with each chamber proposing amendments to the position of the other, or by establishing a conference committee to try to negotiate a compromise version of the legislation.

**Summary of the Report on House of Representatives Legislative Procedures**

The legislative process in the U.S. House of Representatives is governed by a complex set of rules, precedents, and practices, yet understanding these procedures is not as daunting as the sheer volume of documentation might suggest. The official House rules, which exceed 1,000 pages, are supplemented by 30 volumes of precedents, with more expected. Despite this, the House's procedures are largely predictable and follow recognizable patterns, especially in comparison to the Senate. A key principle underpinning these procedures is that the majority of Members should be able to prevail on the floor, with limited opportunities for minority obstruction through filibuster or other parliamentary tactics.

The House has broad authority to determine its own rules, including the power to amend, suspend, or ignore them without consultation with the Senate or President. This flexibility is balanced by the need to manage debate and prevent minority obstruction. For instance, the House imposes time limits on floor debate, with a maximum of one hour per bill and shorter limits under certain circumstances. These limits are enforced through the "previous question" motion, which allows the House to move quickly to a vote after a controlled period of debate.

Most legislative activity occurs in the Committee of the Whole, a body composed of all Representatives that allows for more flexible and extensive debate and amendment processes than the House itself. The Committee of the Whole is often used to consider major bills, with the House adopting special rules to set procedural ground rules, including time limits for debate and amendment, and to determine which amendments are permissible.

Special rules, typically reported by the House Committee on Rules, play a crucial role in shaping the legislative process. These rules can make bills privileged, allowing them to interrupt the regular order of business, and can set specific procedural parameters for debate and amendment. Open rules allow for a wide range of amendments, while closed rules restrict or prohibit amendments, limiting the policy choices available to the House.

When differences arise between the House and Senate versions of a bill, they are resolved either through a "ping-pong" process of exchanging amendments or through a conference committee that negotiates a compromise. Conference reports are then considered by both chambers under special rules, often with limited debate and no amendments allowed.
